text: I'm willing to bet that literally
no one ever climbed out of a Rimac Nevera
and thought, "Oh dear, that needs more power."
And, "I wish it was faster round my local racetrack."
But Mate Rimac can't sit still, and some of the hypercar market
is not convinced by EVs.
So this is how Rimac answers back with the Nevera R.
Now I'll talk you around all the visual tweaks in a moment,
but let's just get straight to the power.
OK. Rimac's Nevera – 1,888bhp.
Nevera R – 2,078bhp.
Now, let's just lay some context on those numbers.
The fastest Ferrari ever around the Fiorano test track is the SF90 XX –
and this has more power than two of them.
And that makes for acceleration numbers that just defy belief.
All your reference points are just blown away.
0-62 is the same as the standard car
because it's limited by what tyres can put on the road.
But it's still 1.81 seconds.
But this thing gets from 0-186mph, or 300kph,
0.6 seconds quicker than that one.
It's also 3.5 seconds faster than  a Bugatti Chiron Super Sport,
1.5 seconds quicker than a Koenigsegg Jesko.
We're used to EVs that blow your mind leaving the line,
but normally they tail off into three figures.
Not this one.
So, how have they done it?
Well, because it's an EV,
I can't just open the bonnet and show you.
But it has got four new motors, which are not just more powerful than that car's,
they've also got the latest, greatest, cleverer version
of that Rimac torque vectoring technology
to share and shuffle the torque  between all four corners.
And the battery powering those motors has also been upgraded.
Capacity is 108kWh, but the chemistry's been changed.
It's lighter, but it's more about giving you that higher sustained performance.
So, you bring it to a racetrack, you can go flat out for longer,
which explains why the bodywork has had these upgrades as well.
So how do you tell someone's got a Nevera R?
Here's the details.
You'll see at the front that that kind of nose cone off the old car is gone.
You've now got this sort of angry gecko face. New front splitter,
entirely different air management around this section of the car,
brakes have been upgraded,
a new silicon layer on your ceramic discs to improve stopping performance,
great big carbon fibre exposed  section in the door here -
looks great – and wider side skirt.
And then you come round to the headline act.
Yes, where your standard Nevera got a modest rear wing,
this one has a monster. Fully exposed carbon fibre, triple supports,
kind of looks like an Aventador SVJ.
And the numbers are geeky. 15% more downforce overall,
10% better aero efficiency, 10% less understeer,
and 3.8 seconds saved on a lap of the Nardò test track.
Now, that is terribly impressive,
except, well, Nardò is a private test track.
It's closed to the public.
We can't go and see a car go round there.
That kind of begs the question, I wonder how fast one of these would go
round Silverstone or Laguna Seca
or the Nürburgring.
Hopefully, one day we will find out, because after all,
the whole point of the Nevera R
is kind of a response from Mate Rimac
to his customers who were saying,
"Yeah, we appreciate that the normal Nevera is a great sort of GT everyday hypercar,
but we'd actually kind of like something
that was a bit more of a ripper around a racetrack."
I have to say though, it really doesn't feel
kind of stripped out and spartan, racetrack-ready in here.
It's still very nicely appointed.
There's a lot more kind of  Alcantara trim instead of leather –
and they've painted the exposed  carbon on the dashboard here
to match the paintwork. But otherwise, seats are comfortable,
there's lots of screens, lots of equipment.
And don't just think it's a kind  of soulless lap time king either,
because you can still twizzle this knob here, select Drift mode
and tell all 2,078bhp to send you sideways.
Madness.
Only 40 Nevera Rs are going to be built,
each costing just shy of £2 million, and I have no doubts that it will happily
smash lap records and rupture internal organs.
It's just funny, though, isn't it?
Even Mate Rimac himself  has said that EV hypercars
aren't selling like V12 or V16 ones are.
Seems crazy, doesn't it?
A machine this wild, numbers this amazing –
but will it be the future of the hypercar after all?
